etymology: Webster 1828 treats MUCH as adjective: great in quantity or amount (Deuteronomy 28:38; 2 Kings 21:6); long in duration; many in number (Numbers 20:20), which last use he marks as no longer current. As adverb: in a great degree; to a great degree or extent (1 Samuel 19:2; Exodus 12); often or long; nearly. As noun: a great quantity; a great deal (Exodus 16; Luke 12). This page fills the KJV-gap measure-word of quantity and degree. Companion pages already treat little, give, and require.
biblical_def: Much in Scripture is not a lifestyle brand and not a vague plenty. It names quantity under God’s hand, degree of love, and the account that follows gift. Manna will not hoard: he that gathered much had nothing over (Exo 16:18). The Lord will not leave stewardship as a slogan: unto whomsoever much is given, of him shall be much required (Luk 12:48). Jonathan will not hide affection: delighted much in David (1Sa 19:2). The forgiven woman will not love as a mood: she loved much (Luk 7:47). The Vine will not baptize independent fruit: the same bringeth forth much fruit: for without me ye can do nothing (Joh 15:5). The dictionary therefore keeps much from becoming either a pile or a vibe. It is the Bible’s way of saying: this much — and then the reckoning.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines MUCH as adjective: great in quantity or amount; long in duration; many in number (obsolete). Adverb: in a great degree; to a great degree or extent; often or long; nearly. Noun: a great quantity; a great deal. He cites Deuteronomy 28:38, Exodus 16, and Luke 12.
webster_full: MUCH, adjective
1. Great in quantity or amount. Thou shalt carry much seed into the field, and gather but little in. Deuteronomy 28:38.
Manasseh wrought much wickedness in the sight of the Lord to provoke him to anger. 2 Kings 21:6.
2. Long in duration. How much time is spent in trifling amusements!
3. Many in number. Edom came out against him with much people. Numbers 20:20. [This application of much is no longer used.]
MUCH, adverb In a great degree; by far; qualifying adjectives of the comparative degree.
1. To a great degree or extent; qualifying verbs and participles. Jonathan, Saul's son, delighted much in David. 1 Samuel 19:2.
2. Often or long. Think much, speak little.
3. Nearly.
MUCH, noun A great quantity; a great deal. He that gathered much had nothing over. Exodus 16.
To whom much is given, of him much shall be required. Luke 12.
scriptures: And when they did mete it with an omer, he that gathered much had nothing over, and he that gathered little had no lack; they gathered every man according to his eating.

But he that knew not, and did commit things worthy of stripes, shall be beaten with few stripes. For unto whomsoever much is given, of him shall be much required: and to whom men have committed much, of him they will ask the more.

But Jonathan Saul's son delighted much in David: and Jonathan told David, saying, Saul my father seeketh to kill thee: now therefore, I pray thee, take heed to thyself until the morning, and abide in a secret place, and hide thyself:
Luk 7:47
Wherefore I say unto thee, Her sins, which are many, are forgiven; for she loved much: but to whom little is forgiven, the same loveth little.
Joh 15:5
I am the vine, ye are the branches: He that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit: for without me ye can do nothing.
corruption_summary: Much is corrupted when quantity is emptied of the Giver, when much-required is recast as self-actualization, and when much fruit is sold as independent productivity.
corruption_paragraphs: The first corruption is pile without manna. Exodus 16:18 gathers much and still has nothing over. The age keeps the heap and drops the omer. Hoard is not provision. The recovery is daily bread.
The second corruption is Luke 12:48 as a brand of potential. Unto whomsoever much is given, of him shall be much required is stewardship under a Lord, not a vision board. Gift is not self-script.

The third corruption is John 15:5 as a growth hack. Much fruit hangs on the Vine. Without Him ye can do nothing. Love in Luke 7:47 is much because sins were forgiven — not because the circle voted intensity.
roots_summary: Webster: quantity / degree (no Latin lemma printed on MUCH). Verse-cache Strong’s on the quotations below: Greek polus (G4183) at Luke 12:48, Luke 7:47, and John 15:5 on much. Exodus 16:18 and 1 Samuel 19:2 carry no Strong’s tag on much in this cache; this page does not mint one.
roots_lines: Greek polus (G4183) — much / many (Luk 12:48, much is given / much required; Luk 7:47, loved much; Joh 15:5, much fruit).
Exodus 16:18 and 1 Samuel 19:2 are KJV-verified; the cache does not tag English much with a Hebrew number on those verse lines. No lemma is invented here.
John 15:5 also tags fruit G2590 beside much; this page does not stretch that number onto leftover cells of other words.
usage: Manna: he that gathered much had nothing over (Exo 16:18).
Stewardship: much given, much required (Luk 12:48); Jonathan delighted much in David (1Sa 19:2).
The forgiven loved much (Luk 7:47); the branch bears much fruit in the Vine (Joh 15:5).

etymology: Webster 1828 treats THOUGH as verb intransitive (tho.): grant; admit; allow. He illustrates from Leviticus 25:35 (relieve him, yea, though he be a stranger), Job 13:15 (though he slay me, yet will I trust), and Proverbs 11:21 (though hand join in hand). Used with as: as though it budded (Genesis 40:10). Familiar trailing though is elliptical. Compounded with all in although. This page fills the KJV-gap concessive. Companion pages already treat trust, faith, and fear.
biblical_def: Though in Scripture is not a shrug and not a branding of resilience. It names the grant of a hard fact under a still-standing Lord. Job will not baptize despair: Though he slay me, yet will I trust in him (Job 13:15). David will not let the valley rewrite the Shepherd: Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil (Psa 23:4). Wisdom will not let conspiracy save the wicked: Though hand join in hand, the wicked shall not be unpunished (Pro 11:21). Mercy will not wait for a kinsman’s papers: yea, though he be a stranger, or a sojourner (Lev 25:35). Charity will not let gifts replace love: though I have all faith, so that I could remove mountains, and have not charity, I am nothing (1Co 13:2). The dictionary therefore keeps though from becoming either stoicism or a meme. It is the Bible’s way of saying: grant the worst — and still the Lord.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines THOUGH as: grant; admit; allow. Used with as (as though). Familiar trailing though is elliptical. He cites Leviticus 25:35, Job 13:15, and Proverbs 11:21.
webster_full: THOUGH, verb intransitive tho.
1. Grant; admit; allow. If thy brother be waxen poor--thou shalt relieve him; yea, though he be a stranger. Leviticus 25:35.
Though he slay me, yet will I trust in him. Job 13:15.
Though hand join in hand, the wicked shall not be unpunished. Proverbs 11:21.
2. Used with as. In the vine were three branches, and it was as though it budded. Genesis 40:10.
3. It is used in familiar language, at the end of a sentence. A good cause would do well though. This is generally or always elliptical.
4. It is compounded with all, in although, which see.
scriptures: Though he slay me, yet will I trust in him: but I will maintain mine own ways before him.
Psa 23:4
Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil: for thou art with me; thy rod and thy staff they comfort me.
Though hand join in hand, the wicked shall not be unpunished: but the seed of the righteous shall be delivered.
And if thy brother be waxen poor, and fallen in decay with thee; then thou shalt relieve him: yea, though he be a stranger, or a sojourner; that he may live with thee.
And though I have the gift of prophecy, and understand all mysteries, and all knowledge; and though I have all faith, so that I could remove mountains, and have not charity, I am nothing.
corruption_summary: Though is corrupted when concession is emptied of the Lord, when valley-walking is recast as mindfulness, and when yet-will-I-trust is sold as grit without a Giver.
corruption_paragraphs: The first corruption is concession without Job 13:15. The age keeps the though and drops the trust. Resilience is not faith. The recovery is yet will I trust in him.
The second corruption is Psalm 23:4 as a breathing exercise. Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death is shepherd-presence, not a wellness glance. The rod and staff are His.
The third corruption is Proverbs 11:21 as networking. Hand joined in hand will not unpunish the wicked. Charity in 1 Corinthians 13:2 stands even though gifts pile high — without it a man is nothing.
roots_summary: Webster: grant / admit (tho.). Verse-cache Strong’s on the quotations below: Greek ean (G1437) at 1 Corinthians 13:2 on though. Job 13:15 and Leviticus 25:35 carry no Strong’s tag on though in this cache; Psalm 23:4 tags the following walk (H3212), not the concessive. This page does not mint a lemma.
roots_lines: Greek ean (G1437) — if / though (1Co 13:2, though I have the gift / though I have all faith).
Job 13:15 and Leviticus 25:35 are KJV-verified; the cache does not tag English though with a Hebrew number on those verse lines. No lemma is invented here.
Psalm 23:4 is KJV-verified; the cache tags walk (H3212) after though, not the concessive itself.
usage: Job trusts though He slay (Job 13:15); David walks the valley though death’s shadow (Psa 23:4).
The wicked are not unpunished though hand join in hand (Pro 11:21).
Relieve the poor though he be a stranger (Lev 25:35); gifts without charity are nothing, though mountains move (1Co 13:2).

etymology: Webster 1828 treats NOTHING as noun from no and thing: not any thing; non-entity; opposed to something; the world created from nothing; no importance; no value (Isaiah 41). As adverb: in no degree; not at all. This page fills the KJV-gap word of non-entity and empty hands. Companion pages already treat world, christ, and prayer.
biblical_def: Nothing in Scripture is not nihilism and not a humblebrag. It names what a man is without the Vine, what the nations are before God, and what he carries in and out of the world. The Lord will not baptize independent fruit: without me ye can do nothing (Joh 15:5). The apostle will not let anxiety play lord: Be careful for nothing (Php 4:6). Gifts without charity collapse: I am nothing (1Co 13:2). The nations will not swagger: All nations before him are as nothing (Isa 40:17). Birth and death will not let a man pack the house: we brought nothing into this world, and it is certain we can carry nothing out (1Ti 6:7). The dictionary therefore keeps nothing from becoming either despair or a pose. It is the Bible’s way of saying: without Him — empty hands.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines NOTHING as noun: not any thing; non-entity; no particular thing; no importance or value (Isaiah 41); a trifle. Adverb: in no degree; not at all. Compound of no + thing.
webster_full: NOTH'ING, noun [no and thing.]
1. Not any thing; not any being or existence; a word that denies the existence of any thing; non-entity; opposed to something. The world was created from nothing.
2. Non-existence; a state of annihilation.
3. Not any thing; not any particular thing, deed or event.
4. No other thing.
5. No part, portion, quantity or degree.
6. No importance; no value; no use. Behold, ye are of nothing and your work of naught. Isaiah 41:11.
7. No possession of estate; a low condition.
8. A thing of no proportion to something, or of trifling value or advantage.
9. A trifle; a thing of no consideration or importance.
NOTH'ING, adverb In no degree; not at all.
scriptures: Joh 15:5
I am the vine, ye are the branches: He that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit: for without me ye can do nothing.
Php 4:6
Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God.
And though I have the gift of prophecy, and understand all mysteries, and all knowledge; and though I have all faith, so that I could remove mountains, and have not charity, I am nothing.
All nations before him are as nothing; and they are counted to him less than nothing, and vanity.
For we brought nothing into this world, and it is certain we can carry nothing out.
corruption_summary: Nothing is corrupted when emptiness is emptied of the Vine, when careful-for-nothing is recast as non-anxiety branding, and when nations-as-nothing is sold as geopolitics without God.
corruption_paragraphs: The first corruption is John 15:5 as a productivity gap. Without me ye can do nothing is union with the Vine, not a missing hack. Independent fruit is a lie.
The second corruption is Philippians 4:6 as a wellness slogan. Be careful for nothing is prayer and supplication with thanksgiving — not a breathing app. Requests are made known unto God.

The third corruption is 1 Timothy 6:7 as minimalism. We brought nothing in and carry nothing out because the world is not the inheritance. Nations in Isaiah 40:17 are as nothing before Him, not before a market.
roots_summary: Webster: no + thing. Verse-cache Strong’s on the quotations below: Greek ou / oudeis (G3756 / G3762) at John 15:5; medeis (G3367) at Philippians 4:6; oudeis (G3762) at 1 Corinthians 13:2 and 1 Timothy 6:7. Isaiah 40:17 tags the following counted (H2803) and later nothing (H657); this page does not mint a leftover lemma.
roots_lines: Greek oudeis (G3762) / ou (G3756) — no one / nothing (Joh 15:5, ye can do nothing; 1Co 13:2, I am nothing; 1Ti 6:7, brought nothing).
Greek medeis (G3367) — no one / nothing (Php 4:6, Be careful for nothing).
Isaiah 40:17 is KJV-verified; the cache tags counted (H2803) and a later nothing (H657, less than nothing). No extra Hebrew number is invented for the first as nothing.
usage: Without the Vine ye can do nothing (Joh 15:5).
Be careful for nothing; pray (Php 4:6); without charity I am nothing (1Co 13:2).
Nations are as nothing before Him (Isa 40:17); we carry nothing out (1Ti 6:7).

etymology: Webster 1828 treats WHILE as noun: time; space of time, or continued duration; worth while = worth the time. As adverb: during the time that; as long as; at the same time that. As verb transitive: to while away time (loiter, or make time pass without irksomeness). As verb intransitive: to loiter. This page fills the KJV-gap word of the open hour. Companion pages already treat day, night, and time.
biblical_def: While in Scripture is not a calendar app and not permission to drift. It names the open hour in which a man must work, exhort, seek, and bless — because the hour closes. The Lord will not let daylight be a mood: I must work the works of him that sent me, while it is day (Joh 9:4). The church will not postpone hardness: exhort one another daily, while it is called To day (Heb 3:13). The psalmist will not save praise for later: Thus will I bless thee while I live (Psa 63:4). Mercy will not wait for a convenient season: Seek ye the LORD while he may be found (Isa 55:6). Sleep will not be neutral: while men slept, his enemy came and sowed tares (Mat 13:25). The dictionary therefore keeps while from becoming either delay or a spa. It is the Bible’s way of saying: this hour — still called Today.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines WHILE as noun: time; space of time; worth while. Adverb: during the time that; as long as; at the same time that. Verb: to while away time; to loiter.
webster_full: WHILE, noun Time; space of time, or continued duration. He was some while in this country.
Worth while: worth the time which it requires; worth the time and pains; hence, worth the expense.
WHILE, adverb
1. During the time that. While I write, you sleep.
2. As long as.
3. At the same time that.
WHILE, verb transitive To while away, as time, is to loiter; or more generally, to cause time to pass away pleasantly, without irksomeness.
WHILE, verb intransitive To loiter.
scriptures: Joh 9:4
I must work the works of him that sent me, while it is day: the night cometh, when no man can work.
Heb 3:13
But exhort one another daily, while it is called To day; lest any of you be hardened through the deceitfulness of sin.
Psa 63:4
Thus will I bless thee while I live: I will lift up my hands in thy name.
Isa 55:6
Seek ye the LORD while he may be found, call ye upon him while he is near:
But while men slept, his enemy came and sowed tares among the wheat, and went his way.
corruption_summary: While is corrupted when the open hour is emptied of work, when today is recast as self-care delay, and when seeking the LORD is sold as a mood window.
corruption_paragraphs: The first corruption is John 9:4 as work-life balance. While it is day is the sent Man’s works. Night cometh. The recovery is work now.
The second corruption is Hebrews 3:13 as a newsletter cadence. While it is called To day is exhortation against the deceitfulness of sin — not a content drop. Hardness waits on delay.

The third corruption is Isaiah 55:6 as a spiritual season. Seek ye the LORD while he may be found is nearness that can close. Matthew 13:25 sleeps; the enemy sows. Psalm 63:4 blesses while I live — not while the feed is quiet.
roots_summary: Webster: time / duration. Verse-cache Strong’s on the quotations below: Greek heos (G2193) at John 9:4; achri (G891) at Hebrews 3:13; en (G1722) at Matthew 13:25 on while. Psalm 63:4 and Isaiah 55:6 tag the following verbs (live H2416; found H4672 / near H7138), not a dedicated while-lemma. This page does not mint one.
roots_lines: Greek heos (G2193) — until / while (Joh 9:4, while it is day).
Greek achri (G891) — until / while (Heb 3:13, while it is called To day); en (G1722) at Matthew 13:25 (while men slept).
Psalm 63:4 and Isaiah 55:6 are KJV-verified; the cache tags live (H2416), found (H4672), and near (H7138) after English while. No leftover Hebrew number is invented for the particle.
usage: Work while it is day (Joh 9:4); exhort while it is called Today (Heb 3:13).
Bless the LORD while I live (Psa 63:4); seek Him while He may be found (Isa 55:6).
While men slept, the enemy sowed tares (Mat 13:25).

etymology: Webster 1828 treats LONG as adjective from Latin longus: extended in a line; drawn out in time; tedious; continued in sound; the long home as the grave (Ecclesiastes 12:5). As adverb: to a great extent in space or time (Proverbs 23; Exodus 19:13); through the whole duration (Genesis 48:15). As verb intransitive: to desire earnestly (Romans 1:11; Psalm 119). This page fills the KJV-gap word of drawn-out time and holy craving. Companion pages already treat life, desire, and salvation.
biblical_def: Long in Scripture is not a playlist length and not a brand of patience. It names the drawn-out hour of refusal, the cry of the forgotten, the years of life God gives, and the ache of holy desire. Pharaoh is not negotiating: How long wilt thou refuse to humble thyself before me? (Exo 10:3). David is not journaling a mood: How long wilt thou forget me, O LORD? for ever? (Psa 13:1). The promise is not a wellness span: With long life will I satisfy him, and shew him my salvation (Psa 91:16). The apostle will not hide the ache: For I long to see you (Rom 1:11). The commandment still carries a land: thou mayest live long on the earth (Eph 6:3). The dictionary therefore keeps long from becoming either delay or a craving app. It is the Bible’s way of saying: this far — and still, how long, O Lord.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines LONG as adjective from Latin longus: extended in line or time; tedious; the long home (Ecclesiastes 12:5). Adverb: to a great extent in space or time. Verb intransitive: to desire earnestly (Romans 1:11; Psalm 119).
webster_full: LONG, adjective [Latin longus.]
1. Extended; drawn out in a line, or in the direction of length; opposed to short.
2. Drawn out or extended in time; as a long time; a long period of time; a long while.
3. Extended to any certain measure expressed; as a span long; a yard long.
4. Dilatory; continuing for an extended time.
5. Tedious; continued to a great length.
LONG home, the grave or death. Ecclesiastes 12:5.
LONG, adverb To a great extent in space; to a great extent in time. They that tarry long at the wine. Proverbs 23. When the trumpet soundeth long. Exodus 19:13.
The God who fed me all my life long to this day. Genesis 48:15.
LONG, verb intransitive
1. To desire earnestly or eagerly. I long to see you. Romans 1:11. I have longed after thy precepts. Psalms 119.
scriptures: Exo 10:3
And Moses and Aaron came in unto Pharaoh, and said unto him, Thus saith the LORD God of the Hebrews, How long wilt thou refuse to humble thyself before me? let my people go, that they may serve me.
Psa 13:1
To the chief Musician, A Psalm of David. How long wilt thou forget me, O LORD? for ever? how long wilt thou hide thy face from me?
With long life will I satisfy him, and shew him my salvation.
Rom 1:11
For I long to see you, that I may impart unto you some spiritual gift, to the end ye may be established;
Eph 6:3
That it may be well with thee, and thou mayest live long on the earth.
corruption_summary: Long is corrupted when duration is emptied of the Lord’s question, when how-long is recast as a complaint brand, and when long life is sold as self-care span without salvation.
corruption_paragraphs: The first corruption is Exodus 10:3 as a negotiation. How long wilt thou refuse to humble thyself is the Lord’s question to Pharaoh. Delay is not diplomacy. The recovery is humble now.
The second corruption is Psalm 13:1 as content. How long wilt thou forget me, O LORD? is petition, not a thread. The hidden face is real. The cry is to Him.

The third corruption is Psalm 91:16 as a longevity plan. With long life will I satisfy him, and shew him my salvation is gift and salvation together. Romans 1:11 longs to impart a gift, not a vibe. Ephesians 6:3 lives long on the earth under commandment — not under a biohack.

David: how long wilt Thou forget me (Psa 13:1); long life with salvation (Psa 91:16).
